intro: The Chinese classics are more than two thousand years old, and they are still alive. They live in translation, where every English word is a choice. They live in calligraphy, landscape painting and tai chi. They live in families at New Year and Qingming, and in films, games and museums. Sometimes they are honored with care. Sometimes they are turned into caricature.

In the first chapter you look at these living texts: how key terms are translated, how art and practice carry the classics, how families and popular culture use them, and how to tell appreciation from caricature. In the second chapter you bring the whole course together in a capstone project on one passage of your choice.

By the end you will be able to establish a text, set it in context, gather three readings from different places, argue your own interpretation with exact citations, and present it to others with the curiosity, precision and respect this course has practiced.
bigQuestion: How do the Chinese classics live today, and how can a careful reader add a fair, well-argued reading of their own?

test.q: Why do translators render dao in many ways?
choices: It means path, speaking, method and more
test.why: Dao carries a wide semantic field.

test.q: Which translator linked Shangdi with God?
test.why: Legge, a missionary scholar, made that link.

choices: A popular but inaccurate word history
test.why: Popular character explanations are often inaccurate.

test.q: Who is honored as the Sage of Calligraphy?
Who does legend credit with creating tai chi?
test.why: Tradition credits the Daoist Zhang Sanfeng; historians trace lineages to the 1600s.

test.q: What is the model minority stereotype?
choices: The idea that all Asian Americans succeed through obedience and study
test.why: Many writers describe it as erasing diversity.

test.q: Where is Chicago's Lunar New Year parade held?

choices: Accurate sources and respect for real practice
test.why: Appreciation understands a tradition as it is.

test.q: What should a capstone research question do?
choices: Ask for a yes or no
Name the passage and a disagreement, and ask why
test.why: A good question focuses the project.

test.q: Which three readings does the capstone gather?
What should a capstone thesis not argue?
choices: Whether a tradition's religious claims are true
test.why: Academic study interprets without ruling on belief.

choices: "The Daodejing describes the Dao as the source of all things."
"The Dao is the source of all things."
test.why: Attributing the claim to the text keeps it descriptive.

test.q: Which English word does Legge use in Daodejing 1 that other translators do not?
test.why: Legge keeps the path meaning of dao with "trodden."

test.q: What should end a capstone presentation, in this chapter's plan?
test.why: An open question fits a subject readers keep debating.

write.prompt: Capstone: choose one passage from the course. Establish the text and translation, set its context, present three documented readings (a classical commentator, a modern reader and a scholar), and argue what the passage means and why its readers differ. Cite every quotation exactly.
tips: Quote only Legge's public-domain translations; paraphrase and label everything else.
Attribute every belief and reading to its holder.
Argue about meaning, not about religious truth.
Use the course's terms with a short gloss the first time.
